opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think information asymmetry was actually one of the biggest things I felt during my time at Tsinghua. People assume that once you get into a top school, everyone has the same opportunities, but that's not really true. The opportunities exist, but whether you *know* about them, and know about them early enough, makes a huge difference.

For example, things like how to get into a good research lab, when you should start reaching out to professors, how summer research programs abroad work, what a strong application for a PhD or master's program actually looks like. Some students come in already knowing all of this, maybe because they have senior friends, or parents in academia, or they came from a high school with a strong network. Other students, especially those from smaller cities, just don't know these things exist until their junior or senior year, and by then it's kind of late.

I think the gap isn't really about intelligence or effort. A lot of people work extremely hard at Tsinghua. The problem is that they optimize for the wrong objective. They focus very heavily on GPA, because that's the signal that's most visible, while the things that actually matter for the next step, like real projects, open-source work, research experience, recommendation letters, are less visible if nobody tells you.

For me personally, one thing that helped a lot was doing open-source projects. When you put your code on GitHub and people actually use it, you get feedback from the outside world, not just from inside the school. That kind of breaks the information bubble a bit, because you start interacting with people from other universities and companies, and you see what they care about.

So if I had advice for younger students, it would be: actively seek out information. Talk to seniors, ask questions that feel "stupid," read about what people did after graduation. And for those of us who already went through it, I think we have some responsibility to share what we learned, because a lot of this knowledge is cheap to give but very expensive to figure out alone. That's partly why I like doing things like this podcast, honestly.

r001.rationale: The response says students who know about opportunities early gain a major advantage, while others may discover them too late; it frames this information gap as consequential during Tsinghua.

r002.rationale: It urges students to seek information and says people who have already navigated the system should share what they learned, supporting broader access to that knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Information asymmetry at Tsinghua was something I only really understood in hindsight. When I was an undergrad, the thing I noticed was that the students who ended up at the top labs, or who got into the best grad programs abroad, were not necessarily the ones with the best grades. They were the ones who knew things early. They knew which professors were actually doing serious research versus just publishing to publish. They knew that you should start doing research in your second year, not your fourth. They knew what a good recommendation letter looked like and who could write one. None of that was taught in any class.

A lot of it flowed through informal channels. Senior students in your dorm, people who had already gone through the application cycle, group chats where someone would casually mention that a certain lab was hiring. If you happened to be plugged into those networks, you got a huge head start. If you weren't, you could be just as talented and still be wandering around not knowing the game existed.

I was lucky in that I got into open source relatively early, and that gave me a different kind of information channel. When you're working on something public, like a reinforcement learning library, you end up talking to people from all over the world who tell you what actually matters in the field. That broke a lot of the local asymmetry for me. I learned from GitHub issues and from random collaborators what people at Berkeley or OpenAI actually cared about, and it was often quite different from what I'd heard on campus.

So my take is that the asymmetry is real and it's a big deal, but it's also increasingly leaky. The internet does a lot to flatten it if you're willing to go out and participate instead of waiting for information to come to you. My advice to students there is always the same: do something visible, put it online, and talk to people outside your immediate circle. The information will start finding you.

r001.rationale: The response describes early access to informal information as a “huge head start” that helped students reach top labs and grad programs, identifying it as an advantage at Tsinghua.

r002.rationale: The response advises students to seek information through open source and wider networks, but does not advocate equal access to information at Tsinghua.

astra-6.text:
I think being at Tsinghua doesn’t mean everyone has access to the same information. You can be on the same campus and still hear about very different opportunities, depending on who you know and what questions you know to ask. Sometimes the biggest gap is simply that you don’t know what you’re missing.

For me, the useful response is to be curious, talk to people outside your immediate circle, and share what you learn. Having access to information is valuable, but knowing how to evaluate it and act on it matters just as much.

r001.rationale: The response describes unequal information access and ways to address it, but does not identify information asymmetry as an advantage for surviving at Tsinghua.

r002.rationale: It encourages sharing what one learns, but does not clearly advocate equal access to information at Tsinghua.

sol-6.1.text:
I think being at Tsinghua gives you access to a lot of information, but access isn’t the same as knowing what to do with it. Even on the same campus, people can have very different ideas about what opportunities exist, who they can approach, or what paths are possible.

Sometimes the gap comes from something quite small—someone has a friend who explains how an application works, while someone else doesn’t even know they’re eligible. So I think reducing information asymmetry means making that informal knowledge easier to share. And personally, it means being willing to ask questions, even when you feel like everyone else already knows the answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes unequal access to opportunities and information, but does not identify information asymmetry as an advantage for surviving at Tsinghua.

r002.rationale: It advocates reducing information asymmetry by making informal knowledge easier to share, supporting more equal access to information at Tsinghua.
